Messages.Author: Mike Nudd
Messages.Body:
First off I figured I'd post afresh as the other massive thread on set
grouping was becoming a little difficult to follow. I really just wanted to
add some constructive thoughts for people to consider/respond to.

Anyway, I have no hesitation in stating that IMHO the set groupings is a
Really Good Idea. Some reasoning has been stated already by various people
on the group, but I figure it is worth recapping. I'll include my additional
comments throughout.

1) GROUPING PROVIDES EQUALITY FOR NEW PLAYERS

Any new player buying into the game now (or in the future) will be able to
take advantage of a play environment with clearly defined boundaries. When
set X is released with crypt cards for group Y, the new player does not
actually need to consider the entire product history of the game, as the
card grouping restricts the play environment to the last few sets still on
print, and the next few sets to be released. More importantly, the new
player does not need to worry too much about his ability to compete with
more experienced players, because these other older players would have to by
necessity either

a) choose from the same limited pool of cards as the new player (hence game
balance), or
b) choose from an alternate limited pool of cards that may in their nature
be different, but which themselves would have defined boundaries in the
interests of fairness and equivalence with other grouping combinations
(hence game balance)

This is a fundamental concept that should encourage more new players to buy
the game, and to participate in official events. The alternative is a more
intimidating environment where more experienced players and collectors have
more options, and more likelyhood of winning both friendly and official
events, which would only scare ambitious new players away.

2) GROUPING PROVIDES THE GAME WITH INNATE CHRONOLOGY

By breaking up card sets into different crypt groups, White Wolf have
immediately given themselves a method for reflecting the passing of time in
the game. When new vampires show up in the RPG setting, they can be produced
also as V:tES cards. When other characters are destroyed in a story, then
they can be cycled out of new card sets. It also means that White Wolf can
move backwards in time to do card sets based on Victorian Age: Vampire, or
Dark
Ages: Vampire.

More interestingly, it raises the possibility of one day seeing less
experienced or more experienced versions of vampire cards (or even crypt
cards) that we already know from the existing card sets we already have
access to. Although this is pure conjecture on my part, is strikes me as a
great way of adding yet more flavour and depth to the game.

3) GROUPING CONSIDERS A CEILING ON CRYPT CHOICE

One important concept of the RPG setting is the fact that the numbers of
active vampires in the world are limited. The ratio is quoted as
approximately 1 to every 100,000 mortals. Furthemore, the world's population
on vampires is further broken up into various clans and sects. It should be
noted that (AFAIK):

- there are more Camarilla vampires than Sabbat or Independent vampires
- there are more Camarilla or Sabbat vampires than Independent vampires
- there are more Camarilla, Sabbat or Independent vampires than there are
bloodline vampires

Not only should there be limited numbers of each clan to choose from in any
crypt grouping combination, but that each combination should observe certain
ratios of choice, as per above. It seems quite appropriate then that instead
of simply adding new vampire cards to a single, massive crypt group, we
instead break things up a bit more.

There then comes the additional advantage that (following the previous point
on chronology above) should WW wish to fundamentally change the distribution
of different vampires in respect to each other in the RPG setting, then this
can be reflected in the card game quite easily by releasing new crypt
groups, as this does not impact on the older vampiers distributions
reflected by card sets already released. E.g. if the Sabbat becomes dominant
in the RPG, then in subsequent groups, there could be more Sabbat vampire
cards printed than Camarilla ones.

With the release of CE, the crypt choice of Camarilla vampires of grouping
combinations 1/2 and 2/3 has already been equalised (15 + 9 vs 9 + 15). In
addition, these figures are equal to the totals of all 4 Independent clans
in Group 2. What we have to ask next is a) what ceiling per sect/clan is
planned by White Wolf for Groups 1, 2 and 3, and what chronological
progression in planned in regards to vampire and clan distributions? In
theory it is possible that White Wolf could choose to release more vampire
cards into the existing 3 groups without moving into a new Group 4 yet.
However, the flip side of this is if the current vampire totals we already
have are to be the ceiling for these groups, then it is possible that any
new vampires for some of the clans in any new sets (including Anarchs) could
be shunted to Group 4 straight away.

It is unlikely that we will be able to draw LSJ or anyone else out on these
design concepts, and so I guess we'll have to wait for new sets to be
released to find which way things go. Either way, I see such developments as
no bad thing.

4) GROUPING KEEPS THE METAGAME MOVING

One additional benefit is that different groupings can break up the
metagame. Different groupings of vampires can be assigned different
distributions of Disciplines and/or card texts. New concepts and card
mechanics could also be released on certain groupings of vampires. Looking
ahead, the grouping system allows White Wolf to segregate different styles
of metagame without restricting the play of the game as a whole.

Also, I doubt I will win many friends by saying this, but the groupings also
gives the VEKN a mechanism for streaming different styles of official play.
By specifying '1/2', '2/3' or '3/4' specific events only, you can encourage
players to try new decks and strategies, rather than just bringing the same
old reliable combo from the same sets to every game all the time. By
changing the competitive environment from event to event, it should be
easier for Princes to keep things interesting for their local player base.

5) GROUPING IS A SUSTAINABLE BUSINESS MODEL

The bottom line is that White Wolf need to make a significant amount of
money from the product line to ensure its future development and
distribution. And although they may be reluctant to admit it, acquiring and
expanding a new player base is probably more important to them than
appeasing the whims of existing, veteran players. The only complication at
the moment is that White Wolf don't have the infrastructure or the
industry/retail presence to market the card game on a world-wide scale
themselves, and so VEKN volunteers (who just happen to be
independently-minded veteran players) are pivotal in the marketing and the
success of the game in the public market.

(The cosmetic design changes to the game aside) White Wolf have actually to
date been very careful not to alienate the existing player base, mainly I
think because of the the symbiotic relationship they currently maintain with
us at the VEKN. The amount of hostility that they have had to deal with in
regards to the changes that came with CE has been unprecedented, and I am
sure from their point of view it has been quite shocking and disheartening.
I think we should all be glad that they have, despite the criticism,
committed to more card sets for Anarchs and beyond. We we originally worried
about Bloodlines before it came out, but the set turned out to be brilliant.
We were all very worried about what we heard about the CE set, but (except
for the cosmetic design) it turned out to be ok. I have every confidence
that White Wolf will continue the handle the product with skill, and with
the player base in mind.

Anyway, the ugly truth is that there is very little future (from a business
perspective) for a game where the play environment is static, such that a
player with some old cards remains as competitive as other players who are
buying into new sets. If the experienced player with a large collection of
old cards can be just as competitive as anyone else, then there is no
incentive for him to buy any new product at all - this does not sustain
V:tES as a business model. In addition, if new players discover they can be
just as competitive by acquiring spares from experienced players, or by
purchasing discounted or second-hand stock of older cards, then again they
will not buy new cards - again this does not sustain V:tES as a business
model.

The best mechanism that keeps people buying cards is to constantly evolve
and change the play environment, and this quite plainly means cycling out a
number of old cards, and introducing a number of new cards in their place on
a regular basis. WotC cracked this business model very early on, and it has
been key to their continued success on the market. My only criticism of WotC
is that the turnaround of their environment for M:tG is so fast is that it
is difficult to keep up as a player without investing a *serious* amount of
money. Too much money IMHO, and as many gamers see this from the outset,
they choose not to buy into the product in the first place. Which is fair
enough.

I think it will be quite necessary for White Wolf to follow a similar model,
but they do not need to make the same mistakes. They have never said that
players can't play with older cards. And, although the VEKN over time might
devote greater energy to promoting newer sets, the old ones will never get
left behind completely. Just like with different M:tG formats, us Princes
could continue to run open format tournaments alongside 1/2, 2/3 specific
events to cater to the different tastes of all the players that are out
there. As long as White Wolf maintain a reasonable pace for the product's
development (i.e. one or two card sets a year at the most) there will be
plenty of time for players to buy in and absorb the latest developments. Or
not as they so choose.

In the long term, White Wolf will have to drive their business model
forward, and either us players will go with them, or we don't. The only
alternative is that they drop the game, and we're back to square one like we
were years ago. From what I've seen in the last 6 months, I think there are
more new players coming to the game with or without the help of us veterans.
The more people buy new product the better, and the more we can encourage
this the better. This is good not just for White Wolf, but for the V:tES
community as a whole, as product lifetime is extended, and future
development and releases are insured.

Well I guess I haven't made many friends by making some of these points, but
I had to get it off my chest. I really do feel us VEKN types need to try to
be more supportive and constructive. I am sure White Wolf would appreciate
reasoned criticism over crazy rants and flames. In fact, I am sure the major
reason that they have made so little announcements to the community over
their intentions for the game is mainly because they feel they got their
fingers burnt unnecessarily the last time around.

And before anyone comments to say what I mindless WW-loving zombie I am, and
how I am ignoring the feelings and criticisms of my local players, all I can
say is that is not the case at all. All of the above is based on my own
independent, reasoned thinking, considering a lot of stuff my players share
with me, and with what I see posted here on the group.

Back in the summer I had a real hard time over the CE, and I had my own
doubts too, but I kept thinking positive, and I held our group together
right up until the CE release. When the set came out there were mixed
reactions, but even the skeptics are now slowly warming to the new cards and
the new concepts. There are a few who can't afford new cards, or they
haven't bought any on principle, but that will always be the case. However
many of us are playing with the new cards, and as a result the play
environment here is changing despite the rest, and it all seems to be going
down well.

Again, some of the guys here have their doubts over what will happen with
the Anarch set. However, that's a long way off yet, and I will voice what I
can with White Wolf in a sensible fashion a little nearer the time. And I'm
pertty sure things will work out for the best.

Anyway, enough from me. I'm outta here.

Regards,

Mike Nudd
VEKN Prince of London

Speaking as a skeptic turned *mostly* skeptic, I'll admit that the grouping

The principle does sound a little scary at the moment, and it's not
something I would advocate in enforcing any time soon. I guess I just wanted
to bat the idea around, as it is something I think the VEKN should tackle at
some point in the future.

As everyone knows, White Wolf have at no point ever said that players can't
use older cards. TBH I seriously doubt it is something they will ever say to
us. Quite frankly they don't really need to. When new card sets are
introduced a good portion of the player community will buy in and will
initially focus on trying the new cards over their older cards for the sake
of novelty as much as any other reason. This is what is already happening
with CE AFAICS. Most of my decks were Group 2-focused with the odd Group 1
vampire here of there. Now my decks are moving from Group 2 to Groups 2/3.
TBH I don't think at the moment I am using any Group 1 vampires in the 16
decks I have currently constructed. TBH I used the old vampires for so long
I'm happy to move on. I may come back later to make the odd 1/2 deck for
nostalgia's sake, or to compete in an open/national event, but otherwise I'm
not fussed.

Given the timeframe for the release of new card sets, it's probably going to
be another couple of years at least before Group 3 is fully populated and we
are will into (theoretically) subsequent Groups. At the moment streaming
events by crypt grouping doesn't actually achieve very much (except maybe
p*** people off), but looking ahead, I can see the advantages for both a)
offering events with more challenge/flavour to players, and b) helping to
promote newer product. If for example if down the line you have a range of
choice between 0/1, 1/2, 2/3, 3/4 and 4/5 decks, then why not try some
combination specific events? And if the range of card sets ends up being so
large, then surely it is reasonable that a certain number of VEKN sanctioned
events should focus just on the latest ones? After all, most sealed events
(including pre-releases) are grouping-specific anyway.

At the end of the day the decision would be down to us as Princes whether to
take this approach or not. You will always have the option of playing with
older cards if you want, and obviously there is no point in fighting your
players if they are not interested (although I'd recommend you seek out some
more co-operative players). It's more a question of whether you want to help
move the play environment and the business model forward or not. I think us
VEKN types have a responsibility to follow this through, and if we don't
then the game will inevitably suffer.

I guess that was the real point underlying the last bit of my earlier post.

Regards,

Mike

I quite agree. However, supposing your local Prince organises and advertises
a sanctioned open constructed tournament, and on the day a couple of new
players show up (whom no-one has met before) with their decks made from the
new cards they recently bought. They would never have seen the older cards,
and they would not have been aware of the principle of veterans giving out
older cards for free. On that day they would still want to play with their
decks, and they would still want to compete on a level playing field. So why
shouldn't we let them, and why shouldn't things be as fair for them as
possible?

In addition, what happens in a couple of years time, when all the veteran
players have given out all their spares of older vampires, and they don't
have any left? New players will (we hope) still be buying into the game at
that point, and again they will want to compete with other players who may
have larger and/or older collections.

Can you see what I mean?

Regards,

Mike

Lots of potential problems.

>And before "dial-a-crypt" gets brought up,

Well, let's start with this.

The game was designed very clearly that you never get the vampires you
absolutely want, unless they're printed. As has been pointed out
before, there would have been potential mileage in a game where the
Methuselah had 30 cards in his crypt and allocated them out to create
vampires who he then paid for, representing a devious, subtle
manipulation and control of a vampire over years, getting them *just*
right. It would also have moved away even further from a Magic like
construct, which was being used as a starting point, swapping carded
creatures for created monstrosities.

You are *supposed* to find it hard to create a crypt. With 15 vampires,
even with 24 vampires (Toreador and Gangrel having duplicates), that was
still difficult. Add more vampires, it gets easier.

At this point, the standard argument is "Well, you could have only added
4 new vampires, then you wouldn't have needed the rule." Potentially
true, but this is LSJ's point of the problem being one of degrees. The
problem becomes more and more pronounced as more vampires are made.
Say, we only create, hmmm, 6 now, and have 9 reprints, well, that's 36
new vampires (42 with Anarchs) for old players. But what if, say,
three, four years down the line, you want to print "The Camarilla Got
Kicked In The Head, Here's the Remains, Suckers"? Print, oh, six or
seven new vampires. You're in the same situation again, it just
happened later. You have 12 new vampires, now.

Each new vampire is obviously themed in clan. No, they don't always
stay true in clan. Obviously not. But there is usually some obvious
facet that makes them Toreador or makes them Giovanni. Yes, we can all
think of exceptions. But it's 90% true - Rake has Brujah disciplines,
Donal O' Connor has some Brujah disciplines, etc.

Assuming current design holds roughly true, you have 12 new vampires.
Some weenies, some middies, some fatties. You get weenies *again*.
Woo, more pre weenies, more cel/pot weenies. For weenies, there are
only so many combinations you can have before you start doing odd
things. A few 'odd' things have come up in Camarilla Edition, just as
in Ancient Hearts etc. But the 'core' is still there. Okay, Gengis is
a bit weird, but you've still got another cel/pot weenie. The amount of
fighting you have to do to get the crypt you want, and adapt around the
limitations, becomes significantly smaller. Alison and Tayshawn, more
cheap cel/pot, or whatever you want. Pile in with the previous vampires
and your crypt stops needing duplicates, becomes even smaller, harder to
contest or whatever. Fun! And it breaks the need to fight for the
right vampires, or use duplicates, which is encoded from the start.

So what if we don't assume current design holds roughly true? Well,
what's the point of clans then?

One of the great splits in the game is that you can do things in clan,
easily, or you can do things out of clan, but much harder. You also
then have much less benefit from, say, a Hunting Ground (some people
swear by them, others at them), an Enchanted Marionette, a Femur of
Toomler or whatever. Any clan card that you want to use becomes much
harder the moment you go cross-clan. Say, you want to play
Presence/Protean. Well, no clan has that in clan, so you fight with
vampires to find what you want. The first six cheapest vampires for it
are 6 different clans (well, 5 plus Caitiff). All the benefits that you
get from staying in clan - early superior disciplines, clan cards, a
tight mix of disciplines and so on - are exchanged for a more carefully
chosen set of disciplines. AUS/CEL/PRE is great, but stealth is hard to
come by. Aus/Obf/Pre might suit you better? A bit all over the place,
and superiors are much harder to come by.

As you add more and more vampires, these limitations become far weaker.
Would we ever get to true dial-a-crypt? Unlikely in the short term, but
eroding the fundamental facets of the game doesn't strike me as a good
idea.

Tap-tap-tap-tap-tap-tap-tap. Anyone wanna place bets on when it falls
over?

Similarly, if some of the vampires in group [63] combo really, really
well with vampires in group [34], what are you going to tell a newbie?
Sorry, we stopped printing those vampires, you'll have to pay 100 quid
just to look at it. Library cards are being recycled and expanded -
pre-cons provide an excellent way of doing that for newbies. But as you
add more vampires, White Wolf have shown a tendency to want story line
vampires. Who's going to be able to get Rake? And if Rake makes that
deck over there uber-competitive, which a newbie can just never get hold
of, what are you going to do? That *does* then turn it into "The person
with the most cards can make harder decks."

Or as you print new expansions, you have to recycle vampires to buggery.
Anyone care to reprint all of Sabbat in 3 years time, when you've
already got 5 full sets of it? Mmm... I can smell the cash flowing out
the door and into another game already.

James Coupe wrote:
>
> You are *supposed* to find it hard to create a crypt. With 15 vampires,
> even with 24 vampires (Toreador and Gangrel having duplicates), that was
> still difficult. Add more vampires, it gets easier.

That may or may not have been an intended feature of the game. In a practical
sense, there's only so many vampires WotC could have issued in the first edition
of the game. And given the number of disciplines they were forced to allow for
various reasons, the original level of difficulty in determining the crypt was
set by an artifact caused by undeniably practical reasons. This is not a good
reason to suggest that it (or something like it) must be defended as a perpetual
game feature going forward - except possibly in a "devil-you-know" type of
argument.

And frankly, it's a feature I've never cared for. At least, the difficulty of
creating a decent crypt for a given deck concept has often struck me as being
greater than it needs to be. I don't like having to decide between the
relative handful of deck archetypes that have a ready, riskfree crypt for them
and branching out into more imaginative strategies that almost inevitably involve
risk of either vampire duplication or drawing fairly poor choices in some of your
games. When you opt for the latter, certain games will get lost on the shuffle
of the crypt deck, thus throwing off the entire table balance for the game. I've
always felt that risk of a bad crypt draw was one of the poorer design properties
to use in to balance this game. Of course, I would still concede that you have to
use it at some level because I also agree that the true "Dial-A-Crypt" scenario
would lose something for the game as well. I just feel like there was never a
risk of getting to a point where a player could chose a truly arbitrary
combination of disciplines and still easily build a crypt for it.

> So what if we don't assume current design holds roughly true? Well,
> what's the point of clans then?
>
> One of the great splits in the game is that you can do things in clan,
> easily, or you can do things out of clan, but much harder.

But who said things were going to be easy to do out of clan just because
more vampires are allowed in combination? A few things will be. But with
the choices in different levels of different disciplines and different
specials, there are limitless numbers of vampires that can be issued
without replicating, say, some weird Chi-Dom confluence in the more or
less the same capacity vampire 12 times - unless it's replicated in
rather high-cap vampires. I think we've found over time that using whole
crypts full of high-cap vampires are not worth using just for the ability
to pull off some strange combo. In fact, historically that's been one of
the weaknesses of the game as designed: high cap vampires are not even
attractive for the number of different discipline combinations they
allowed for. Ultimately, attractive specials need to be grafted onto
them to get players to use them. That point is very revealing about the
real danger (or lack thereof) of arbitrary combo disciplines, IMO.

> AUS/CEL/PRE is great, but stealth is hard to
> come by. Aus/Obf/Pre might suit you better? A bit all over the place,
> and superiors are much harder to come by.
>
> As you add more and more vampires, these limitations become far weaker.

Marginally weaker. Not "far weaker". At least in my experience, over
time from Jyhad only through all the expansions that have been issued,
I haven't seen evidence of any kind of detrimental shift except possibly
in the availability of weenies in a given discipline. Even these are a
creep, not a rush. And I don't care about them. If they become too
much of a factor, I'm sure a few more antiweeny cards that have alternate
use might be called for but nothing major.

> Would we ever get to true dial-a-crypt? Unlikely in the short term, but
> eroding the fundamental facets of the game doesn't strike me as a good
> idea.
>
> Tap-tap-tap-tap-tap-tap-tap. Anyone wanna place bets on when it falls
> over?

Yea. I'll take 21 million years from now. Assuming the current rate of
expansions of course. But I'm crude. I'm perfectly willing to foist
this problem off on my great great great great great (time some order of
magnitude) grandchildren.

Fred

With the existing skills I can think of at least two problems with this
approach. The first is that "unusual discipline combos" would create a CE set
which is inferior to its predecessors. If the CE is a hodge-podge of odd skills
then the new players without access to VTES/Jyhad would be disadvantaged.

to mismatched) skills (like say Venture with Animalism) than were previously
introduced, you'd be degrading what I call the "clannishness" of each clan.
Printing Ventrue with Animalism, Gangrel with Presence, Toreador with Protean,
etc. makes each clan less distinct. Eventually "clan" becomes meaningless when
you widely distribute what gives each of them their distinctness. The
degradation probably wouldn't reach an unacceptable level for most people for a
while but I believe it is a flaw in that approach.

I do think that you are probably right and that the design team could have
developed a set that worked with the concepts you've mentioned to create a CE
set. Unfortunately, the suggestions above are only attempts to ignore the
problem or delay dealing with them. The design team seems to have decided that
a new CE base set would be a good time to address the problem. The grouping
rule actually *addresses* the problem and provides a way for countless numbers
of cards to be produced long into the future.

-Robert
